overview.headline: Trade backlash starts on the farm, and cues move opinion fast
overview.standfirst: Eight papers clear the bar this week. The strongest match for the trade preferences project is a 127-country study tying rural protectionism to uncompetitive agriculture; the immigration and fiscal project gets a Swedish study of non-citizen voting and local taxes.

sections.head: Where trade attitudes come from
sections.body: {W4414116330} argues that rural voters back protectionist parties and policies where local agriculture lacks comparative advantage, using harmonized surveys from 127 countries and post-NAFTA variation in the US. The abstract does not say which survey programs are merged, so coverage of Latin America is worth checking. {W7222506786} finds that offshoring by US multinationals raises incumbent vote share in counties with more educated workers and lowers it where manufacturing and offshorable occupations are common; it is US only and county level, not individual attitudes. {W7223458148} uses the MITA dataset to show that worker mobility clauses in trade agreements follow economic interdependence and path dependence, not migration control goals.

sections.head: Immigrants, refugees and the public purse
sections.body: {W7113383583} studies Sweden's 1975 reform giving non-citizens the local vote and finds a one-time rise in municipal income taxes, larger where foreign voters were a bigger share and concentrated in closely contested municipalities. It speaks to fiscal outcomes of immigration through political power rather than attitudes. On attitudes, {W7224807583} finds in a 2024 US survey experiment that Americans associate refugees and immigrants with different themes but show no difference in warmth, affect or policy preferences. {W4414761356} finds in Pakistan that coethnicity raises acceptance of Afghan refugees mainly among hosts who are a minority in their province. Neither attitude paper measures fiscal concerns.

sections.head: Cues work quickly and depend on the messenger
sections.body: {W7225174171} uses a US strike announcement that fell during a fielded survey and finds partisan divergence in support for military action within minutes. {W7224876078} runs a survey experiment in five European countries (n = 10,513) and finds that anti-IO populist cues lower support for multilateral aid, and that the same message from a mainstream party lowers support across the spectrum, while bilateral aid is unaffected. Both bear on cues as shortcuts, the mechanism in the political trust project, though neither concerns trade or Latin America. {W7224821017} reports a field experiment in Brazil where legislators sided more often with a business group when its size and economic weight were emphasized.

sections.head: Redistribution and the Latin American economy
sections.body: {W7224115010} uses eight redistributive ballot initiatives in six US states and finds lower- to upper-middle-income precincts more supportive than upper-income ones, with the largest class gap in Republican precincts. {W7224930453} develops a concept of peripheral monopoly capital from four Chilean business groups; it is theoretical and qualitative, not about opinion. For data, {W7223808300} introduces a database of 38 non-reciprocal preference schemes from 1950 to 2025 and finds export gains only for least developed countries, and {W7224848391} builds structural gravity measures of trade dependence and finds Chinese aid has raised partners' dependence on China without the reverse.

flagged.why: Trade preferences: rural voters support protectionist parties and policies where local agriculture is uncompetitive, shown with harmonized surveys from 127 countries and post-NAFTA variation in the US.
Multinationals and voters: links employment at foreign affiliates of US multinationals to incumbent vote share, positive in more educated counties and negative in manufacturing counties. US only.
Immigration and fiscal outcomes: Sweden's 1975 non-citizen local franchise produced a one-time rise in municipal income taxes, concentrated in closely contested municipalities. Outside Latin America.
Immigration attitudes: a US survey experiment finds different beliefs about refugees and immigrants but no difference in affect or policy preferences. US only, no fiscal measures.
Elite cues and IPE attitudes: a five-country European survey experiment finds anti-IO populist rhetoric from mainstream parties lowers support for multilateral aid across the spectrum.
Trade and migration policy: new MITA data show worker mobility clauses in trade agreements follow economic interdependence and path dependence, not migration control goals.
Redistribution preferences: revealed support in eight US redistributive ballot initiatives tracks precinct income, with the largest class gap in Republican precincts. US only.
Partisan cues: minute-level exposure to a US strike announcement during a survey shows partisan divergence in opinion within minutes. US only and on military policy, not economic policy.

high_signal.why: APSR article offering structural gravity measures of trade dependence that account for intermediates and substitutes, useful for any IPE work that uses interdependence as a variable.
APSR field experiment in Brazil showing legislators respond to business groups' signals of size and economic importance, a causal test of informational lobbying in Latin America.
RIPE article theorizing Chilean business groups as the organizational base of dependency, relevant to debates on concentrated capital in Latin American political economy.
New database of 38 non-reciprocal trade preference schemes from 1950 to 2025, with gains found only for least developed countries.
Journal of Politics study showing coethnicity with refugees raises host acceptance mainly where hosts are a provincial minority, qualifying cultural threat accounts of immigration attitudes.

notes: NBER, SSRN, SocArXiv, IMF and World Bank working papers returned no items in this window, nor did Latin American Politics and Society, Revista de Ciencia Política or Política y Gobierno, so Latin American and working paper coverage is thin this week.
